extracted.intended_audience: comics creators, small-press publishers, festival organizers, and general readers interested in the Ignatz Awards
extracted.subtask_description: Information about the Ignatz Awards: categories, selection mechanism, jury/committee composition, and the award's stated purpose (what kinds of comics the prize aims to honor). Useful for creators or organizers who want to understand how works are evaluated or categorized for the Ignatzes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Award mission / purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: To honor the work of indie comics and graphic novel creators whose work 'challenges popular notions of what comics can achieve, both as an art form and as a means of personal expression.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This expressed purpose indicates a qualitative preference for independent, experimental, or boundary-pushing work rather than mainstream/commercial comics. Examples of winners across years illustrate the kinds of indie/artist-driven projects the award highlights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection mechanism — festival ballot
rubrics_metrics.description: The Ignatz is a festival prize determined by a ballot of attendees and exhibitors of the Expo.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because winners are chosen by SPX attendees and exhibitors, results reflect the perspective and environment of the Expo; the page notes the results are 'unique to the environment found at the Expo.' The Expo steering committee previously decided not to hold the awards in 2001 because they couldn't ensure similar voting conditions offsite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-nomination policy / permissibility
rubrics_metrics.description: There were 'no rules against self-nomination' (noted in the controversy where a juror nominated his own book).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page documents a controversy over self-nomination (Frank Cho nominated his own work in 1999) and criticism from Ed Brubaker about lack of guidance to judges; this indicates historically permissive practice and potential conflicts of interest that have shaped perceptions of legitimacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ignatz Awards Jury (juror selection and role implied)
rubrics_metrics.description: A listed set of jurors for various years (e.g., Jessica Abel, Chester Brown, Ed Brubaker, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page enumerates jurors year-by-year, implying a role for named industry professionals in the awards process (nomination, adjudication, or oversight). The presence and makeup of the jury serve as a quality-control / credentialing factor for nominations and decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ignatz Awards Committee / coordinators (organizational oversight)
rubrics_metrics.description: Named coordinators and committee members across years (e.g., Chris Oarr, Jeff Alexander, Eden Miller, Dan Stafford).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Committee composition and coordinator continuity affect administration, rules, and implementation of the awards (e.g., cancellation decisions, publication of guidelines). Organizational stewardship is an implicit criterion for how the awards are run and how rules are applied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Category: Outstanding Series
rubrics_metrics.description: Award category recognizing an ongoing/serialized comics series (e.g., winners listed by year such as Acme Novelty Library, Love & Rockets).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page lists nominees and winners yearly, giving concrete examples of series considered outstanding. The category implicitly evaluates sustained quality across multiple issues/volumes rather than a single issue or short work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Category: Outstanding Comic
rubrics_metrics.description: Award category recognizing an individual comic issue or standalone comic (e.g., Eightball #17, Hey Mister #1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nominees/winners shown by year indicate emphasis on a specific issue or single comic as a unit of evaluation. Examples across years illustrate the form and editorial/creative approaches that have been honored.

rubrics_metrics.name: Category: Outstanding Minicomic
rubrics_metrics.description: Award category recognizing minicomic-format works (small-press, self-published short comics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page provides many year-by-year winners and nominees, signaling the award's attention to small-format, often self-published work. Examples show that self-published and DIY minicomic projects are considered within this category.

rubrics_metrics.name: Category: Outstanding Online Comic
rubrics_metrics.description: Award category recognizing webcomics/online-published comics (e.g., American Elf, Achewood, Hark! A Vagrant).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Yearly lists demonstrate recognition of digital-native comics and serial online work; criteria implied include quality of storytelling and art in an online presentation and community impact among SPX attendees/exhibitors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Category: Outstanding Anthology or Collection (discontinued)
rubrics_metrics.description: Award category that recognized anthology volumes or collected works (listed as discontinued on the page).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include curated anthologies and collected works; the 'discontinued' label indicates the category existed historically and that criteria focused on editorial curation and compilation of multiple contributors or stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Category: Outstanding Graphic Novel or Collection (discontinued)
rubrics_metrics.description: Award category recognizing graphic novels or collections (page marks this category as discontinued in later years).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Winners like It's A Good Life if You Don't Weaken and Blankets illustrate the category's emphasis on longer-form, book-length comics. Discontinuation indicates award categories have evolved over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Category: Outstanding Debut Comic (discontinued)
rubrics_metrics.description: Award category intended to recognize a creator's debut work (listed as discontinued).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples (where present) show the award once explicitly recognized first works, signaling a criterion that elevates promising new talent; discontinuation means the category is not consistently applied across years.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of historical examples as evaluative guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: The page lists nominees and winners by category and year, serving as an implicit criterion bank for what types of work the Ignatz honors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Creators and publishers can use the provided winners/nominees as exemplars to infer quality standards, stylistic tendencies, and the kinds of editorial and creative risks that have succeeded at SPX voting and juried selections.
